analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare Advantage plans to make prior-authorization decisions faster, electronically, and publicly reported.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Medicare Advantage prior-authorization bill with 231 cosponsors — more than half the House — died in committee without ever getting a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets the prior-authorization system used by Medicare Advantage plans, where insurers decide before treatment whether they will pay for a service or item, and delays or denials can leave seniors waiting for care. It would require plans to accept prior-authorization requests electronically instead of by fax or proprietary portals, meet Secretary-set response deadlines such as 24 hours, and publish plan-by-plan data on approval rates, denials, appeals, turnaround times, and use of artificial intelligence in decisions. It would also let the government waive prior-authorization paperwork for doctors who consistently follow the rules and require a public report on fast-tracking decisions for services that plans routinely approve.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans, who would see faster and more transparent decisions on whether their insurer will cover care, and the doctors and suppliers who currently spend hours submitting and chasing prior-authorization paperwork. The bill's public reporting would also let beneficiaries compare how often each plan denies or delays care before they enroll.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors in Medicare Advantage plans and their doctors

how_it_helps.text: Plans that use prior authorization would have to operate a standardized electronic program, and a fax, a proprietary portal that fails Secretary-set standards, or an electronic form would no longer count — replacing the slow, non-standard channels providers deal with today.

The Secretary could set binding response deadlines — such as 24 hours — for prior-authorization decisions, including expedited requests, instead of relying on the current 72-hour standard for the narrow cases where it applies.

Plans would have to report annually to the government and to a public CMS website, plan by plan, what services required prior authorization, approval and denial rates, how many denials were appealed and how many appeals succeeded, average and median response times, and their use of artificial intelligence and automated decision-making in these determinations.

Plans would have to adopt enrollee protection standards, including letting doctors with strong track records skip or lighten prior-authorization requirements and reviewing the list of services requiring approval each year with input from enrollees and providers.

CMS and the health IT office would have to report by January 1, 2027 on defining and implementing real-time decisions for routinely approved services, and a GAO evaluation of the program would follow by 2028.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers would bear the cost of building electronic prior-authorization systems, collecting and publishing detailed data, and processing decisions under possible 24-hour deadlines — and public denial-rate data would expose the plans with the highest denial rates. Some of those compliance costs could flow into premiums or plan offerings.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not ban or restrict prior authorization itself or the use of AI in making decisions — plans could still deny care under the same criteria; they would just have to do it faster, electronically, and in public view.
The mandates are back-loaded: transparency reporting begins in 2026 and electronic prior authorization in 2027, so seniors would see no change for at least a year after enactment.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that compliance costs fall on insurers, who may pass them to enrollees through premiums or reduced plan extras, and that the electronic-system mandate creates costs and technical burdens for smaller providers and plans alike.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but incremental: faster decisions, standard electronic submission, and public denial data are meaningful for seniors stuck waiting for care and for doctors drowning in paperwork, and public reporting lets beneficiaries shop plans with better information. But the bill regulates the gatekeeping system rather than loosening it — denials, AI-assisted decisions, and insurer discretion all remain, with the fixes delayed until 2026 and 2027. It is a well-aimed, moderate improvement that leaves the underlying structure untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees in June 2024 and, six months later, was sent to a Health Subcommittee — it never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Kelly (R-PA) introduced the bill on June 12, 2024, with a large bipartisan group of original cosponsors, and it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee.
The bill drew 231 cosponsors in total — 140 Democrats and 91 Republicans — well over half the House.

The only action after referral was a December 17, 2024 referral to the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health; neither full committee ever held a markup or vote, and the House never took the bill up before Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers are better off because the bill died: their prior-authorization process remains as-is, with no electronic submission mandate, no Secretary-set response deadlines, no public reporting of denial rates, appeals, or AI use, and no real-time decisions for routinely approved services. Seniors waiting on coverage decisions and doctors managing fax-based prior authorization gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare Advantage insurers, whose prior-authorization process stays intact

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: of 231 cosponsors, 140 were Democrats and 91 were Republicans, and the sponsor was a Republican — yet the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: Prior authorization stays in place and these plans remain the gatekeepers of care — the bill locks in their role while subjecting it to electronic processing mandates, possible 24-hour response deadlines, and public plan-by-plan reporting of denial and appeal rates. Their interest in continuing to profit from denial-based cost control runs against enrollees' interest in fast access, which is exactly what the reporting requirements would expose.

Doctors and suppliers would submit prior-authorization requests through a standardized electronic system rather than fax or proprietary portals, could qualify for waivers from requirements based on their track record, and would gain access to plans' coverage criteria and required documentation. These gains track directly with faster care for their patients.

industries.industry: Health IT and electronic prior-authorization vendors
industries.note: The mandate that every prior-auth plan build a standards-compliant electronic transmission program would create a market for the software and infrastructure to run it. The benefit to patients depends on the systems actually speeding decisions.
